pull.title: net: allow selecting BIP152 high-bandwidth peers with `-addnode`
pull.body:
Bitcoin Core automatically selects up to three BIP152 high-bandwidth peers after they deliver new blocks. This works well for ordinary connections, but it cannot use topology information known to the operator.

For example, an operator may run nodes in multiple locations, or maintain a stable, low-latency link to another node, and want that peer to announce compact blocks immediately and consistently, including after reconnects, instead of waiting for automatic selection.

This PR adds a `bip152hb` net permission:

```
-addnode=203.0.113.5 -whitelist=bip152hb,out@203.0.113.5
```

For a peer with this permission, the node requests high-bandwidth mode in the existing `SENDCMPCT` message sent at `VERACK`, so it applies to every connection to that peer and requires no new P2P messages. It works with the existing `-whitelist`/`-whitebind` semantics: `out` applies to manual connections (`-addnode`, `-connect`, `addnode` RPC), `in` (the default) to inbound connections, and subnets are supported. Matching is by IP address or subnet, so hostnames are not supported.

Peers with the permission are additional to the three automatically selected high-bandwidth peers and never take one of their slots. This intentionally allows explicit configuration to exceed BIP152's current three-peer recommendation and may increase redundant bandwidth. If accepted, BIP152 can be updated separately.

Notes:
- `bip152hb` is not included in `all`: unlike the other flags it grants the peer nothing and only costs bandwidth, so existing `all@` configurations are unaffected.
- The permission is rejected at startup with `-blocksonly`, where high-bandwidth mode is never requested.

Earlier versions of this PR used an `-addnode=<host>=bip152-hb` suffix; it was reworked into a permission following review (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35940#issuecomment-6811490029).

Concept ACK

The opt-in override of the BIP152 three-peer cap seems fine to me, since it's an explicit operator choice, not a default, and it's disclosed upfront.
Reusing `-addnode` also made more sense to me than creating a dedicated option.

Concept ACK

I think it’s a good addition to let users add their own high-bandwidth peers, as it gives them more control. I was initially worried about there being no cap on the number of user-selected high-bandwidth peers. However, since this will mostly be used by advanced users, it only affects the operator's own node, and the release notes already warn about the extra bandwidth, I think it's okay to leave it as is.
Concept ACK, but I think it might make more sense to do this as a whitelist permission.

events.message:
net: add bip152hb permission flag

Add a "bip152hb" permission that can be granted with -whitelist and
-whitebind, and that is reported by getpeerinfo. The next commit uses it
to request BIP152 high-bandwidth compact block announcements from such
peers, so operators can apply topology knowledge (for example a
low-latency link to another node they run) that the automatic
high-bandwidth peer selection cannot have.

Unlike the existing flags, this one grants the peer nothing and only
makes us request extra announcements. It is therefore not part of
"all", which would otherwise increase bandwidth usage for existing
configurations.

The flag has no effect yet.

events.message:
net_processing: request high-bandwidth mode from bip152hb peers

Bitcoin Core automatically selects up to three BIP152 high-bandwidth
peers after they deliver new blocks. That selection cannot use topology
information known to the operator, e.g. a stable low-latency link to
another node they run, which should announce compact blocks immediately
and consistently, including after reconnects.

For peers with the bip152hb permission, request high-bandwidth mode in
the SENDCMPCT message sent at VERACK, so that this applies to every
connection to such a peer. Keep these peers out of
lNodesAnnouncingHeaderAndIDs: they are additional to the three
automatically selected peers and must not displace them. As for the
automatic selection, never request high-bandwidth mode in -blocksonly
mode.

Combined with the existing "out" whitelist direction, this lets an
operator configure an added node as high-bandwidth, e.g.
-addnode=203.0.113.5 -whitelist=bip152hb,out@203.0.113.5

The cmpctblock fuzz target asserted that there are at most three
high-bandwidth peers. Only count automatically selected ones there, and
check that peers with the permission are high-bandwidth once the
handshake completes.

init: reject bip152hb permission with -blocksonly

High-bandwidth compact block announcements are never requested in
-blocksonly mode, because our mempool would not contain the transactions
needed to reconstruct the blocks. Fail at startup when -whitelist or
-whitebind grants the bip152hb permission in that mode, rather than
silently ignoring the operator's configuration.
doc: add release note for bip152hb permission

events.body:
Thanks @davidgumberg for the suggestion! I've reworked the PR to add a `bip152hb` permission instead of the `-addnode` suffix:

```
-addnode=203.0.113.5 -whitelist=bip152hb,out@203.0.113.5
```

The diff is a lot smaller now: there's no extra `-addnode` parsing and no code to match connections against added nodes.
 
As a bonus, it now also works with the `addnode` RPC and `-connect`, can cover several nodes with one subnet entry (e.g. `bip152hb,out@10.0.0.0/24`), and can apply to inbound connections from those addresses.

Two trade-offs:
- Whitelist entries only match IPs and subnets, so an addnode given as a hostname, or a connection made through a name proxy, can no longer get high-bandwidth mode.
- `bip152hb` isn't included in `all`: unlike the other flags it grants the peer nothing and only costs us bandwidth. It's also rejected with `-blocksonly`, where high-bandwidth mode is never requested.

I think losing hostnames is acceptable so I pushed a new version.

Following the same pattern as in the `test_empty_addnode` in line 268 of the same file, I think we could also check the case where an -addnode` is empty but carries the suffix `bip152-hb` (`-addnode==bip152-hb`).
```suggestion
        with node.assert_debug_log(expected_msgs=["Ignoring empty -addnode value"]):
            self.start_node(0, extra_args=["-blocksonly", "-addnode==bip152-hb"])
        util.assert_equal(node.getaddednodeinfo(), [])
```
